sections.overview: The fire salamander is a robust, long-tailed amphibian of Europe whose life joins damp woodland with freshwater nurseries. Most adults live on land, while their offspring begin life as gilled larvae in streams or pools. This split means a healthy population needs both sheltered ground and suitable water within reach. Its conspicuous pattern and secretive habits make it easier to recognize than to observe.
sections.identification: An adult has a broad head, stout trunk, four short limbs and a rounded tail; in Central Europe adults commonly measure about 14-17 cm from snout to tail tip, with larger individuals reaching around 20-23 cm. Females tend to be heavier and slightly larger, especially when carrying embryos. The smooth, glossy black back bears irregular yellow spots or bands, sometimes orange or reddish; each pattern is distinctive, but its exact form varies among individuals and regions. Skin glands release secretions containing toxic alkaloids, including samandarine and samandarone. These chemicals can deter predators, but do not prevent every attack. In the Central European subspecies S. s. terrestris, adult males are usually 14–16 cm and under 20 g; females are usually 15–17 cm and over 20 g, exceeding 50 g when carrying larvae.
sections.habitat: Across much of its range, the species favours deciduous and mixed woodland with cool, moist soil, leaf litter and hiding places such as dead wood, rock gaps and root hollows. Adults shelter by day and may roam through the forest floor at night, so a stream alone cannot provide the habitat they need. Females use springs, headwater streams and sometimes ponds or other still waters to release larvae; local choice depends on what water bodies are available. Forest cover, clean water and connected refuges together make a usable landscape.
sections.diet: On land, adults hunt small invertebrates such as earthworms, woodlice, beetles and slugs, swallowing each prey whole. Aquatic larvae hunt small water-dwelling animals, especially insect larvae.
sections.behavior: The salamander is mainly nocturnal and becomes easier to see on rainy nights, when its skin is less exposed to drying. Adults breathe air with lungs, while aquatic larvae use external gills; in dry weather adults seek cool crevices, burrows or shelter beneath logs. During courtship, males may compete or interfere with rivals near a female.
sections.reproduction: Mating takes place on land: the male courts the female at close range and deposits a gelatinous spermatophore on the ground, which she takes up with her cloaca. Sperm is stored inside her, so fertilisation is internal; after gestation, she usually enters shallow water and releases fully formed, gilled larvae rather than laying eggs there. Many populations give birth to several dozen larvae, but two localized Iberian lineages independently evolved births of near-metamorphosed or fully terrestrial juveniles. In Central Europe larvae commonly metamorphose in roughly 40–120 days, losing their gills as lungs and limbs support life on land; timing changes with water conditions and food.
sections.ecology: In pond-breeding populations, larvae prey on aquatic invertebrates and can affect local food webs. In a studied pond-adapted Central European population, females brought nutrients from land into ponds with their broods, and metamorphs carried some biomass back onto land; the return was smaller than the initial input because many larvae died and survivors were small. Larvae and adults are themselves food for other predators, although an adult’s glandular secretion can make it an unpalatable meal.
sections.conservation: The global IUCN Red List classifies Salamandra salamandra as Vulnerable; the assessment was made on 26 July 2022 and published in 2023, so its category is not a current count at every site. Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans, or Bsal, is a chytrid fungus that infects skin and has been linked to severe, documented population declines in the Netherlands and Belgium. At Het Bunderbos in the Netherlands, one population fell by about 99.9% within seven years of the suspected introduction. EFSA notes that the historical route into Europe is not established and that a causal link between Bsal and declines in wild populations is not always clear; amphibian trade is a suspected pathway. Habitat loss, road deaths and drained springs threaten some populations.
